title: Solomon asks (1 Kings 3)
hook: offered anything, a young king asks for an understanding heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, David weeping above the gate: my son Absalom. Your line was would god I had died for thee. Who in your family did you reach toward? Day four hundred seven, and a new week.
screen: `WOULD GOD I HAD DIED FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: If God appeared to you tonight in a dream and said, ask whatever you want, what would you ask for? Be honest. Money that would end the worrying. A long, healthy life. Somebody's mind changed. It happens to a young man named Solomon, David's son, newly king. He has gone to the high place at Gibeon to offer sacrifice, and that night the Lord appears to him in a dream and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Ask what thou wilt that I should give thee." No limits. Solomon's answer is today's word.
screen: `ASK FOR ANYTHING.` → `A NEW KING AT GIBEON.` → `ASK WHAT THOU WILT.`

segments.voice: Solomon starts with honesty. "I am but a child, and know not how to go out and come in." He's king of a huge people and he doesn't know how to begin. So he asks: "Give therefore to thy servant an understanding heart, to judge thy people, and discern between good and evil." In Hebrew it's even more striking. Solomon asks for a lev shomea, a listening heart. The same word as the boy Samuel's thy servant heareth. Wisdom, in this story, starts with listening. And God is pleased. Because you didn't ask for long life, or riches, or your enemies' lives, he says, I give you a wise and understanding heart, and the things you didn't ask for too. Then, right away, the chapter shows what that heart looks like. Two women come before the king, sharing one house, each with a newborn. One baby died in the night. Both claim the living child. No witnesses. Solomon calls for a sword: divide the living child in two. One woman says, fine, divide it. The other cries out: give her the child, just don't kill him. And Solomon knows the mother: the one who would rather lose her son than see him die. That's wisdom here: not cleverness, but seeing into a heart. The Catholic Bible keeps a whole book in Solomon's voice, the Book of Wisdom, one of the seven books Catholics count in the Old Testament that many Protestant Bibles leave out or set apart. In it, the speaker remembers this moment: "I called upon God, and the spirit of wisdom came upon me." And the Church counts wisdom first among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.
screen: `I AM BUT A CHILD.` · `A LISTENING HEART.` · `TWO MOTHERS AND A SWORD.` · `THE BOOK OF WISDOM.` · then, large: `GIVE THY SERVANT AN UNDERSTANDING HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for wisdom today. Settle, and breathe. Think of one decision on your plate where you honestly don't know how to go out and come in. A conversation you dread. A choice at work. Something with your kids or your parents. Now, instead of asking for the outcome you want, ask for a listening heart about it. If you pray, you can use Solomon's words: give thy servant an understanding heart. Then listen. To the people involved, to your own conscience, to the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Wisdom. In Hebrew, chokmah: the gift Solomon asked for, a listening, understanding heart that can tell good from evil. Today's word.
Your line: an understanding heart. Today, before one decision, listen longer than feels efficient. Day four hundred seven.

howItsDone: Catholics read the Book of Wisdom, one of the deuterocanonical books, in the Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours, and count wisdom first among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit received in confirmation.

fork.setup: you're Solomon. two women claim the same baby, there are no witnesses, and everyone is waiting for the king's judgment. what do you do?
options: ask the neighbors who they believe.
call for a sword and order the child divided.
give the baby to the woman who spoke first.
fork.reveal: he calls for a sword. one woman agrees; the other begs him to give the child away alive. Solomon gives the baby to her: she is the mother.

original.note: Hebrew: wisdom, skill for living well. In Greek, sophia; in the Latin of the Church, sapientia.

trapdoor: what you thought: wisdom means being smart.
what it means: Solomon asks for a heart that listens and tells good from evil, and proves it by reading a mother's love.
what a scholar hears: lev shomea, a hearing heart. and the Book of Wisdom, in the Catholic canon, retells the request in Solomon's voice.

notes: Hebrew lev shomea (1 Kings 3:9): confirm. The link to Samuel's 'thy servant heareth' (day 398) is the shared root shama.
The Book of Wisdom is written in Solomon's voice (chapters 7–9) but is not attributed to him by most modern scholars; the script says only 'in Solomon's voice'. Confirm.
Deuterocanonical books: described as books 'Catholics count in the Old Testament that many Protestant Bibles leave out or set apart'. Confirm the wording is fair to both.
CCC 1831 lists the seven gifts with wisdom first; confirm.
The Douay names 1 Kings as 3 Kings; refs give both.
